title: Sensor placement: data wrangling using DSL allocation layer
text: This document prepares the inputs used by sensor_placement.qmd and the optimization scripts (python/sensor_site_optim.py, python/biodiv_site_optim.py): it starts from an allocations layer (ESRF_Allocations_20260825.gpkg) sent by Kaitlyn Athearn on 25 August 2026, builds a grid of candidate sensor locations with their environmental covariates, and computes distance to the nearest road. This document must be rendered before sensor_placement.qmd, since the latter reads the files written here rather than re-deriving them.

title: Sensor placement: data wrangling using DSL allocation layer
text:
1 Loading the raw data
I start from the ESRF_Allocations_20260825 layer stored in ESRF_Allocations_20260825.gpkg provided by K. Athearn and use the stand and watershed attributes therein.






Important



The most up-to-date allocation information is in the ops_allocation field of this layer and not the hcp_allocation field, which reflects historical allocations. This version of the document uses the ops_allocation field.




Code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import geopandas as gpd
from skimpy import clean_columns
from pyprojroot.here import here

f = here('Data/esrf_alloc/ESRF_Allocations_20260825.gpkg')
bio_f = here(
    'Data/esrf_alloc/biodiv_sites/'
    'ESRF 2023 Biodiversity Surveys_AdjustedSiteCentersInverts.shp'
)
roads_f = here('Data/esrf_alloc/ESRF_roads_ODF.gpkg')

# load data
esrf = gpd.read_file(f, layer='ESRF_Allocations_20260825')
bio_sites = gpd.read_file(bio_f)
roads = gpd.read_file(roads_f)

esrf = clean_columns(esrf)
bio_sites = clean_columns(bio_sites)
roads = clean_columns(roads)

# convert ops_allocation values to snake_case 
esrf['ops_allocation'] = (
    esrf['ops_allocation']
    .str.replace(r'[^0-9a-zA-Z]+', '_', regex=True)
    .str.lower()
)

# convert hcp allocation to snake case
esrf['hcp_allocation'] = (
    esrf['hcp_allocation']
    .str.replace(r'[^0-9a-zA-Z]+', '_', regex=True)
    .str.lower()
)

# convert treatments to snake case
esrf['hcp_ws_assignment'] = (
    esrf['hcp_ws_assignment']
    .str.replace(r'[^0-9a-zA-Z]+', '_', regex=True)
    .str.lower()
)

# remove riparian buffers from consideration
esrf = esrf.loc[
    ~esrf['ops_allocation'].str.contains(r'_rca', regex=False),
    :
]










Figure 1: Map of stand allocations based on DSL (ops_allocation) allocations as of August, 2026. Riparian conservation areas have been masked, except for inside the CBMA-CRW watersheds, where additional geoprocessing is necessary.











Important



Note that the CBMA-CRW polygons include what was allocated as RCA. I am not sure if this was by design or if the RCA polygons need to be clipped from the CBMA-CRW polygons.

2 Computing proportion of each watershed allocated to the triad levels

Figure 2: Ternary plot of watersheds and proportion of each allocated to one of three management types. Note that the grey points represent other watersheds not assigned to a treatment in the original design.





The important take-aways from Table 2 and Figure 2 are that the Triad-E watersheds have been pushed towards higher proportions of reserve than the original design. This indicates that a regression-type approach, using mixture models may be better than considering the watersheds as belonging to the original treatment designations. I therefore use the proportions of area allocated to each stand treatment type to redesignate the watershed treatments. For example, watershed 26 must be reassigned from Triad-E to CRW (reserve).






Important



I use the watershed treatment types (CRW reserve, Intensive, Triad-I, Triad-E, and Extensive) as a starting point to ensure the initial placement of sensors spans a good range of the triad experiment, but use a regression approach with continuous measures of proportions of each watershed type in defining the objective function for the optimization scheme. The watershed treatment assignments below are therefore just a construct to aid in visualization and initialization.


To reassign watersheds to original treatment constructs, I define a band around the Cox direction for the Extensive treatment Figure 3. Treatments are then designated by the proportion of Extensive, with less than 5% as Intensive, between 5% and 40% as Triad-I, between 40% and 80% as Triad-E, and more than 80% as Extensive. Those with more than 95% reserve are designated as control/reserve watersheds. Watersheds falling outside the band around the Cox direction are left unassigned but elligible for sensor placement (colored purple in Figure 3).


Code
# redesignate the watersheds based on where they fall in the ternary
# plot above. Watersheds with no original assignment, or assigned
# crw_partial, keep their original hcp_ws_assignment value. A watershed
# is only assigned one of the triad classes if it falls within a band
# around the reserve == intensive diagonal; its sub-class is then
# determined by prop_extensive. This mirrors classify_triad() below,
# used to trace the same boundaries over the full simplex.
eligible = (
    triad['hcp_ws_assignment'].notna()
    & (triad['hcp_ws_assignment'] != 'crw_partial')
)
in_band = (triad['prop_reserve'] - triad['prop_intensive']).abs() <= 0.2

triad['triad_trt2'] = np.select(
    condlist=[
        eligible & (triad['prop_reserve'] > 0.95),
        eligible & in_band & (triad['prop_extensive'] < 0.05),
        eligible & in_band & (triad['prop_extensive'] >= 0.05) & (triad['prop_extensive'] < 0.4),
        eligible & in_band & (triad['prop_extensive'] >= 0.4) & (triad['prop_extensive'] < 0.8),
        eligible & in_band & (triad['prop_extensive'] >= 0.8),
    ],
    choicelist=['crw_full', 'intensive', 'triad_i', 'triad_e', 'extensive'],
    default=np.where(eligible, 'none', triad['hcp_ws_assignment'])
)










Figure 3: Ternary plot of watersheds using the updated triad_trt2 designations, with the decision boundaries from the redesignation rule overlaid (dashed lines). Shaded regions show where each rule applies across the full simplex; points show the actual watersheds.













Figure 4: Visual of the spatial arrangement of guiding “treatments”. The watersheds that fell outside of the original Triad design after adjustments are now labeled as “unassigned”. These will still be considered during sensor placement, but not used in the strict backbone of the original placements.





The stand-level allocations determine the columns of \(\mathbf{X}\) (the proportions of reserve, intensive, and extensive), but we want to make sure that we don’t accidentally confound environmental conditions with the triad experiment when choosing the sensor locations. To do this, we add a DEM raster to get elevation, slope, and aspect. We also use the stand age as another control variable to help determine placement.

title: Sensor placement: data wrangling using DSL allocation layer
text:
3 Terrain covariates
Elevation, slope, and aspect are derived from a 30 m DEM (USGS 3DEP, via py3dep), smoothed and downsampled to a 120 m grid, in python/get_course_dem.py. That script writes a 4-band raster (elevation, slope, aspect_x, aspect_y) to Data/esrf_alloc/dem_esrf_120_terrain.tif, which I load here.








Figure 5: Terrain covariates derived from the 120 m DEM: elevation, slope, and aspect (decomposed into x/y components).





Using the centroids of each 120 m grid cell in the landscape, we extract the geospatial data to a spatial points data frame. This provides a list of candidate locations at which to locate sensor nodes.

title: Sensor placement: data wrangling using DSL allocation layer
text:
4 Creating the candidate site data


Code
from shapely.geometry import Point

esrf_proj = esrf.to_crs(dem_120_terrain.rio.crs)
# simplified stand-level allocation, for stratifying site placement by
# stand allocation within a watershed treatment (see ALLOC_SIMPLE_MAP above)
esrf_proj['alloc_simple'] = esrf_proj['ops_allocation'].replace(ALLOC_SIMPLE_MAP)
# attach per-watershed treatment proportions so candidate_locs carries them too
esrf_proj = esrf_proj.merge(
    triad[['hcp_wtr_shd_id', 'prop_intensive', 'prop_extensive', 'prop_reserve', 'triad_trt2']],
    on='hcp_wtr_shd_id',
    how='left'
)
bio_proj = bio_sites.to_crs(dem_120_terrain.rio.crs)
roads_proj = roads.to_crs(dem_120_terrain.rio.crs)
eus_proj = eus.to_crs(dem_120_terrain.rio.crs)

# Build spatial points from the terrain raster's cell centers
xs = dem_120_terrain.x.values
ys = dem_120_terrain.y.values
elev_vals = elevation.values
slope_vals = slope.values
aspect_x_vals = aspect_x.values
aspect_y_vals = aspect_y.values
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
x_ind, y_ind = np.meshgrid(
    range(len(xs)),
    range(len(ys))
)

nodata = dem_120_terrain.rio.nodata
mask = (elev_vals != nodata) if nodata is not None else np.ones(elev_vals.shape, dtype=bool)

candidate_locs = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {
        'elevation': elev_vals[mask],
        'slope': slope_vals[mask],
        'aspect_x': aspect_x_vals[mask],
        'aspect_y': aspect_y_vals[mask],
        'index_x': x_ind[mask],
        'index_y': y_ind[mask]
    },
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(xx[mask], yy[mask]),
    crs=dem_120_terrain.rio.crs
)

# Spatial join: attach triad polygon attributes to each point in the grid
candidate_locs = gpd.sjoin(
    candidate_locs,
    esrf_proj[[
        'geometry', 'age_2020', 'triad_trt2', 'ops_allocation',
        'alloc_simple', 'hcp_wtr_shd_id', 'prop_intensive', 'prop_extensive',
        'prop_reserve'
    ]],
    how='left',
    predicate='within'
)
# drop the 'index_right column'
candidate_locs.drop('index_right', axis=1, inplace=True)

# conduct a spatial join with the biodiversity sites
## first grab the columns we actually want
bio_proj_cols = ['station_id', 'geometry']
bio_proj_sa = gpd.sjoin(
    bio_proj[bio_proj_cols],
    eus_proj[['hcp_wtr_shd_id', 'geometry']],
    how = 'inner',
    predicate = 'within'
)
bio_proj_sa.drop(['index_right', 'hcp_wtr_shd_id'], axis = 1, inplace = True)

# now find the nearest candidate to each biodiv site within
# the study area
bio_div_join = gpd.sjoin_nearest(
    bio_proj_sa,
    candidate_locs.reset_index(names = "cell_id")[['cell_id', 'geometry']],
    how = 'left'
)
bio_div_join.drop(['index_right'], axis = 1, inplace = True)
bio_div_join.rename({'geometry': 'geometry_bio'}, axis = 1, inplace = True)

# now join these back to identify which cells contain the the biodiv sites
candidate_locs = bio_div_join.join(candidate_locs, on='cell_id', how="right")

# fill the nas in the station_id
candidate_locs['station_id'] = candidate_locs['station_id'].fillna('none')
# only keep the grid cell locations (i.e., "snap" the biodiv monitoring sites to the grid cell centers)
candidate_locs.drop(['geometry_bio'], axis = 1, inplace = True)
candidate_locs = candidate_locs.dropna()

# create filter mask
mask = np.array(np.repeat(1, candidate_locs.shape[0]), dtype = 'bool')
mask[candidate_locs['triad_trt2'].isna().values] = False
mask[
    (candidate_locs['triad_trt2'] == 'crw_partial')
    .values
] = False

# filter out the treatments we are not interested in
candidate_locs = candidate_locs[mask]










Figure 6: Candidate locations with the watershed boundaries overlaid. Note that the partial wartersheds do not get considered.





Next step is to compute, for each point, the distance to the nearest road based on the roads layer.


Code
candidate_locs = candidate_locs.sjoin_nearest(
    roads_proj,
    'left',
    distance_col = "dist_to_road_m"
)
candidate_locs.drop('index_right', axis=1, inplace=True)

title: ESRF Triad Design
text: Reports for the Elliott State Research Forest (ESRF) Triad experimental design: selecting sensor placements that span environmental conditions while dovetailing with the Triad management allocation (intensive / extensive / reserve) and existing biodiversity surveys.

title: ESRF Triad Design
text:
Reports

Sensor placement plan — the sensor-siting optimization and results.
Data wrangling: DSL allocation — inputs built from the current DSL allocation layer (run first).

title: Sensor placement plan
text:
We want to identify sensor node locations that span a range of environmental conditions, are human-accessible (i.e., close to roads), while also dove-tailing with existing research, including the biodiversity assays and the triad design. Specifically, suppose we wish to fit the model \[
y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^\top {\boldsymbol \gamma} + (\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{Z}_i){\boldsymbol \beta} + \epsilon_i
\] to some response \(y_i\) measured at the sub-watershed scale such that \(i\) indexes the sub-watershed. The 3-vector, \(\mathbf{x}_i\), measures the proportion of each triad management scheme, intensive, extensive, and reserve, planned for the subwatershed, while \(\mathbf{Z}_i\) is an \(n_i \times p\) matrix of control variable measurements within sub-watershed \(i\). These represent the multiple conditions over which we want take measurements across the study region. The vector \(\mathbf{a}\) determines the aggregation strategy over the measurements within a subwatershed. For example a vector of length \(n_i\) with elements \(\mathbf{a} = (1/n_i, 1/n_i,...)^\top\) would average the measurements of a given control variable across the sensors within a subwatershed. The vector \(\boldsymbol \beta\) contains the coefficients for the aggregated control variables and \(\epsilon_i\) is a random error term.
Assume for now that the Triad design is fixed such that \(\mathbf{X}\) is known. The objective is to maximize the variability of environmental conditions captured by the sensor locations across the study area while also minimizing confounding with the triad proportions, all under logistical constraints. One option here is to maximize the minimum eigenvalue of the empirical information matrix:
\[
O(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Z}_1, \mathbf{Z}_2,...) = \lambda_{\text{min}}(\mathbf{M}^\top \mathbf{M}) - \gamma_r \sum_{i,j} \phi({d_{ij}})
\] where \(\lambda_\text{min}({\mathbf W})\) denotes the minimum eigen value of a square matrix \(\mathbf{W}\), \(\underset{(n \times (p + 3))}{\mathbf{M}}\) is the columnwise concatenation of \(\mathbf{X}\) and \(\underset{(n \times N)}{\mathbf{A}}\underset{(N \times p)}{\mathbf{Z}}\), where \(\mathbf{A}\) are the aggregation vectors arranged along rows such that row one contains the elements of \(\mathbf{a}_1\) in the columns \(1,2,...,n_1\), with zeros elsewhere, row two contains the elements of \(\mathbf{a}_2\) in the columns \(n_1 + 1, n_1 + 2,..., n_1 + n_2\), and so on. The matrix \(\mathbf{Z}\) contains the control variable measurements for each location on the landscape in rows and different control variables in columns. Finally, \(d_{ij}\) is the distance of site \(j\) within sub-watershed \(i\) from the nearest road while \(\phi\) is a desired transformation and \(\gamma\) is a penalty factor. Both \(\gamma\) and any parameters defining \(\phi\) are hyperparameters that can be tuned.
Here, I use \(\lambda = 1\) and \(\phi(\cdot) = \exp(\theta d_{ij}) - 1\) with \(\theta = \log(0.5) \times 10^{-3}\) such that no penalty is incurred if the site is adjacent to a road, but the penalty increases to an amount that is virtually insurmountable given the scale of the minimum eigenvalue once the design point is placed more than 1 km from the road.

title: Sensor placement plan
text:
2 Data wrangling
Several data wrangling steps were necessary to build a set of candidate sensor locations with the environmental covariates needed for the objective function above. For this analysis, I started with the ESRF_Allocations_20260825.shp layer provided by Kaitlyn Athearn on 25 August 2026, the 2023 biodiversity survey site centers (from Maggie Hallerud), and the ODF roads layer (from T-drive). This section summarizes those steps and their results, while the full process can be found on the data wrangling page.






Figure 1: Spatial arrangement of the triad treatments across sub-watersheds.




2.1 Terrain covariates
Elevation, slope, and aspect come from a 30 m DEM (USGS 3DEP, via py3dep). The script python/get_course_dem.py smooths this DEM, downsamples it to a 120 m grid, and derives slope and aspect from it, decomposing aspect into x/y components to avoid the ‘wraparound’ issue at 360\(^\circ\) / 0\(^\circ\).


2.2 Building the candidate location grid
Using the centroids of each 120 m grid cell in the landscape, I built a spatial points data frame of candidate sensor locations, then attached the triad treatment of the sub-watershed containing each point, stand age in 2020 from the DSL stand inventory, and, for cells that contain an existing biodiversity monitoring site, that site’s station ID (existing biodiversity sites are “snapped” to their containing grid cell’s center). Candidate locations falling in “partial” sub-watersheds were dropped since they were not part of the experimental design. Finally, I computed each candidate location’s distance to the nearest road, used in the road-proximity penalty described above.
The resulting candidate locations and sub-watershed/treatment layers are saved to Data/sensor_optim/data_for_optim.gpkg (layers candidate_locs and esrf), along with the reprojected biodiversity site locations (layer bio_sites), for use by the optimization scripts and the results below.






Important



Because the potential sensor locations are located at the center of the grid cell, they will not align exactly to the biodiversity plot centers, even if the chosen sensor locations indicates it is “at the biodiversity site center”. Instead, it will simply be the grid location nearest to the indicated biodiversity plot.

title: Sensor placement plan
text:
3 Two ways to optimize
Depending on how flexible we want to be in adhering to the existing biodiversity plot network, we can optimize the above objective function in multiple ways. The first option below relaxes the strict adherence to the biodiversity plots and only uses them as a starting point, while the second option finds the “best” network design, constrained to the biodiversity plot locations.

3.1 Grid-based stochastic search
For the more flexible, grid-based option, we search over the dense 120 m DEM grid of candidate locations built above, proposing moves to spatially adjacent grid cells (@note-alg1). This is useful when sensor locations are free to be placed almost anywhere on the landscape.






Algorithm 1




Initialize random starting locations.

for t in treatments:

Assign a minimum of \(n_t\) sensor sites to treatment \(t\). Randomly select a polygon assigned to treatment \(t\).
Select the next polygon assigned to treatment \(t\) at random out of those that are not adjacent to any of those already selected.
If a non-adjacent watershed is not available, select the next polygon uniformly at random from those assigned to treatment \(t\) and those that remain unassigned (purple watersheds in Figure 1).

For each selected polygon, select a candidate location uniformly at random out of those that share a cell with the biodiversity sites (this starts the algorithm near biodiversity sites, then allows it to expand to “better” locations).

Set starting difference at a default value, diff = 999.
while diff > tol for a set tolerance tol:

for s in sites:

Propose 1 of \((2r + 1)^2 - 1\) possible jumps to an adjacent grid cell, where \(r\) serves as a sort of “radius” in the discretized grid determining how large a neighboorhood to consider in the proposals.
if the proposed grid cell lowers the objective function, then accept the proposal and exchange site s for the proposal.
else keep site s

end for
Compute the reduction in the objective function as diff.
Increment counters

end while.




3.1.1 Implementing Option 1: Grid-based stochastic search
This optimization routine can be run using the python script sensor_site_optim.py. This requires two datasets:

The candidate locations, which is a grid of spatial points with all the attributes derived above, created in the data wrangling report.
The sub-watershed polygon layer with triad treatment designations (experimental units data, eus).

3.1.3 Notes to review

I used weights to allocate sites to triad treatment–stand allocation combinations such that each sub-watershed type (CRW, Intensive, Triad-I, Triad-E, and Extensive) received four sensor nodes. Within each sub-watershed type, I distributed sensor nodes evenly across the stand allocation types (reserve, intensive, extensive) based on how many stand types are available in a given watershed type (e.g., only reserve and intensive stands exist in intensive watersheds). For Triad-I watersheds, the fourth sensor node was randomly assigned to a stand type. For Triad-E waterhsheds, the fourth sensor node was selected out of the unassigned wathersheds that used to be Triad-E.
There is not currently any criterion to help ‘spread points out’ in space. This could be added, but selecting non-adjacent experimental units is the only constraint to limit spatial clustering at the moment.
I used a ‘jump radius’ of 2, meaning that the algorithm could ‘try out’ 1 of any in a 5 \(\times\) 5 grid (minus the center cell) in an attempt to improve the objective function. I didn’t notice much difference across runs when playing around with changing this parameter.
Based on some initial exploration, I noticed that the trailing eigen-values tended to be between about -0.5 and 3.5. I therefore set the distance penalty such that there was zero penalty for being at a road (distance = 0 m) and increasing exponentially, incurring a penalty of 3 at 1 km. This should make it very unlikely that any candidate locations are selected if they are more than 1 km from a road. We can adjust this as needed.




3.2 Option 2: Exchange search over existing biodiversity sites
Rather than searching a dense grid, this option restricts the candidate set to the sites that are already existing biodiversity monitoring stations, and picks the ‘best’ 20 of those. Because the candidate set is small and fixed, the search proceeds as a direct exchange algorithm instead of a grid-neighbor random walk:






Algorithm 2




Draw an initial set of 20 sites from the fixed biodiversity site pool.

These initial draws are done through stratefied random sampling, sampling from each watershed \(\times\) stand treatment combination as described in @note-alg1.

Set starting difference at a default value, diff = 999.
while diff > tol for a set tolerance tol:

for s in sites:

Evaluate swapping site s for every currently-unselected candidate in the pool.
Accept the single best swap for s if it improves the objective function; otherwise keep s.

end for
Compute the reduction in the objective function as diff.
Increment counters

end while.



The candidate pool itself is built from the raw biodiversity survey site locations (213 points), joined to the sub-watershed/triad-treatment layer and filtered down to 183 sites that fall inside a triad-assigned sub-watershed (sites outside the triad allocation or within ‘partial’ sub-waterhseds, were excluded). Elevation, slope, aspect, and stand age are borrowed from the nearest already-computed 120 m grid cell center (candidate_locs); distance to road is computed exactly at each site’s coordinate. During each step, a site can be swapped in for the current site if it falls in the same watershed \(\times\) stand allocation treatment combination and also improves the objective function.

3.2.1 Running the optimization routine






Note



Code for this option can be found in python/biodiv_site_optim.py, which draws its core search routine (exchange_search()) from python/biodiv_site_optim_lib.py.
